notes.meaning: Israel packed up their tents at Mithkah and set up camp at Hashmonah. Most of these desert stops are not mentioned anywhere else in the Bible, showing how God led His people through quiet, hidden stretches of the wilderness. God never lost track of them, guiding each step from one camp to the next.

The people journeyed from Hashmonah to Moseroth. Moseroth is another form of the name Mosera, near the place where Aaron was later buried. Even when the people moved across barren land without a permanent home, the Lord kept directing their journey.

Israel moved on from Moseroth to Bene-jaakan, a location known for the wells dug by the descendants of Jaakan. Finding water was essential in the desert, and God brought the large camp to places that could sustain them. He faithfully provides for His people even in dry and difficult seasons.

From Bene-jaakan, the nation traveled to Hor-haggidgad, a place named for deep hollows or caves. This location appears in other passages under a shorter name, Gudgodah. God continued to guide the camp safely through rough and broken land.

Israel left Hor-haggidgad and pitched their tents at Jotbathah. Scripture elsewhere describes Jotbathah as a refreshing area with running streams and brooks. God brought His weary people to cool waters right in the middle of the arid steppe.

The camp left the waters of Jotbathah and moved south toward Abronah. Little is known about this stop today, but it marked another stage on their long journey toward the Red Sea. God cares about every step His people take, even those that seem ordinary or forgotten.

Israel moved from Abronah to Ezion-geber, an ancient harbor located at the northern tip of the Gulf of Aqaba. This is one of the few places in this list that can be identified with certainty today, and it later served as a port for King Solomon's ships. After decades of wandering, God was still keeping His covenant people alive and together.

The Israelites traveled north from Ezion-geber back to Kadesh in the Wilderness of Zin. Kadesh was the famous site where Israel had previously sent out twelve spies and then turned back in fear. Returning here marked the end of their long wilderness detour and the start of a new chapter for the next generation.

Israel marched from Kadesh to Mount Hor on the border of Edom. Edom refused to let the people pass peacefully through their territory, forcing Israel to camp along the edge of the mountains. God protected the camp as they skirted the borders of neighboring lands.

Aaron obeyed God's word by climbing Mount Hor, where he died as the high priest near the end of Israel's forty years in the wilderness. This is the only place in the Bible that records the exact date of his passing, in midsummer on the first day of the fifth month. Even in the solemn hour of his death, Aaron followed God's command in quiet obedience.

Aaron lived to be 123 years old before the Lord called him home. He was three years older than his brother Moses and had served the people through many long trials since leaving Egypt. His long life was a clear sign of God's kindness and special blessing over many decades.

The king of Arad, who ruled in the southern desert of Canaan, learned that Israel was approaching his borders. This brief note recalls an earlier battle where this king attacked Israel and took prisoners before God granted Israel victory. It reminded the people that they were arriving at the edge of the promised land and would soon face real conflict.

After mourning Aaron on Mount Hor, the Israelites moved on and pitched camp at Zalmonah. The route took them around the territory of Edom through rugged desert terrain. God remained with them as they began the final stage of their march toward Canaan.

Israel packed up their tents at Zalmonah and journeyed to Punon, located in the region of Edom. Good camping sites in this dry eastern area were rare and far apart. God faithfully led the vast congregation from one outpost to the next.

The people traveled from Punon to Oboth on their journey northward. The name Oboth refers to water skins, hinting at a place where travelers gathered water for their desert trek. God continued to sustain the bodies and spirits of His people as they drew nearer to their goal.

Israel moved from Oboth to Iye-abarim, a site whose name points to rocky ruins or small hills along the border of Moab. Reaching this border showed that the desert wandering was nearly finished and brought them close to the Jordan River. God was bringing His ancient promises closer to fulfillment day by day.

Israel left Iyim and set up camp at Dibon-gad along the river valleys east of the Dead Sea. This town was later settled and rebuilt by the tribe of Gad, which gave the site its full name. God was now leading His people right through lands they would soon possess.

Moving north from Dibon-gad, the people camped at Almon-diblathaim in Moabite territory. This town is also mentioned by later prophets when describing the plains of Moab. Step by step, God was guiding the nation toward the very spot where they would cross into Canaan.

Israel climbed into the high range known as the Abarim Mountains, camping right across from Mount Nebo. From these heights, Moses would soon look out over the promised land before his death. The high vantage point allowed Israel to gaze down toward the final destination God had prepared for them.

Israel came down from the mountains and spread their camp across the low plains of Moab, just across the Jordan River from Jericho. This was the final major base camp for the rest of Numbers and the entire book of Deuteronomy. Here God prepared His people for the river crossing and the tasks ahead.

The camp stretched out for miles along the Jordan River, from the town of Beth-jeshimoth all the way to Abel-shittim. Abel means mourning, recalling the sorrow Israel felt there after falling into sin at Peor. The camp stood as a living reminder of God's patience, discipline, and mercy over forty years.

While the people rested by the Jordan across from Jericho, the Lord gave Moses new instructions for the nation. This marked the start of the legal rules that would govern the conquest and division of Canaan. God speaks directly to His people so they know how to live in obedience when entering His gifts.

Moses was told to speak to the whole congregation about what must happen once they crossed the Jordan River into Canaan. The commands looked forward to the moment their feet touched the promised land. God wanted them fully prepared in heart and mind before they crossed the water.

God commanded Israel to clear the land of its pagan residents and destroy every carved stone, metal statue, and hilltop altar. High places were outdoor shrines on hills where people offered sacrifices to false gods. Israel had to remove all traces of false worship so that their own devotion to the one true God would not be corrupted.

The Lord commanded Israel to move in, clear out the previous owners, and live in the cities and homes. They were not taking the land by their own strength, but receiving it as a direct gift from God, who owns the whole earth. God gives His people an inheritance so they may rest in His promises and serve Him faithfully.

The land was to be divided fairly among the tribes by drawing lots, matching the size of the territory to the size of each clan. The lot ensured that the location was decided by God rather than human favoritism, preventing jealousy between tribes. God cares about justice and provides an appropriate place for every family under His care.

God warned the people that if they showed false mercy or grew lazy and left Canaanites in the land, those survivors would cause constant pain. Like sharp thorns in the side or splinters in an eye, these neighbors would tempt Israel into idol worship and bring constant trouble. Harboring compromise with sin always leads to pain and deep spiritual harm.

God solemnly warned that if Israel adopted the wicked ways of the Canaanites, He would bring the same judgment on them that He planned for their enemies. Instead of keeping the land, Israel would be driven out and sent into exile. God is completely just and holds His own people accountable to His holy standards.
